utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed I can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution,.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, Senior Trial Attorney. Together with me co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Vasvija Vidovic together with Mr. John Jones on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We are joined today which our legal assistant Ms. Jasmina Cosic and our case manager Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, last week we discussed your request for a map, an overview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, we talked about it yesterday after we finished the sitting. Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We finalised that in such a way that we can provide you a black-and-white copy of one map, so merging together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's excellent, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have here now the copies with me and I would like to tender this. My first reaction is to tender as such, and then I thought shouldn't be an exhibit for the Prosecution, but if you didn't raise it, I wouldn't have asked the mapping unit to do so. It's referring to your request and highlighting or circling the places named in the indictment excepted two hamlets who couldn't be traced as such, but it is a request by Chambers. So I suggest it might be an exhibit for Chambers, but I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I agree 100 per cent. Do you have any suggestions to that, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first we should have a look at that map to see what they actually marked on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But apart from that, that stands to reason. Apart from that, we take it that this will be a Trial Chamber document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In addition to that, Your Honour, the two hamlets named are near Ratkovici, the hamlets not on the map that are circled like that are Bradjevina and Gornji Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will find them. Don't worry. We have Ratkovici? We have. So this will be -- yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor, in fact, marked the places referred to in the indictment. Therefore, we have no objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be document TC1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's okay. I don't want to quarrel with you on an extra letter. I mean, definitely not, not on Friday. Had it been Monday, I would have made a casus belli out of it, but on Friday you win the day. Anything further from you, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yesterday we filed the motion on our response on judicial notice of adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And with a view to the witness list, we filed yesterday -- there was a request from Chambers to -- to have Mr. Gow available for a week rather than three days. Meanwhile, we contacted Mr. Gow in that regard, the question to be available, and it is a fact that he is not available for a whole week. He is available for the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th of November. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's a week earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, that's not a week earlier. Oh, you mean like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is a week earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's Friday, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He is available for those three days. If it should be three days and if it should be a week then we should reschedule but this is a tentative schedule list, so we will further refine and update you then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But if the Chamber asks us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he is available only 22nd, 23rd, 24th that basically is barely enough to cover the three days that the Defence said they require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I suppose you require him here for a day, a day and a half or a few hours. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It will be part of a trial day for two hours, two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to take the risk of them not finishing with him. Though I have my own opinion. I could dispose of that witness in less than one sitting as the -- as the indictment stands now, but anyway. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we believe that we shall not require longer than two days with Mr. Gow, I mean. We'll try to organise ourselves in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if it's two days the Defence and one day you, you can bring Mr. Gow over 22nd. 22nd is Monday. We start with him, and we finish him off on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic, for telling us that. The other thing is this: We've gone through your response to the Defence motion on taking adjudicated facts from the Deronjic case. Considering the opposition and considering the nature of the facts that the motion of the Defence suggests ought to be taken into -- taken into consideration as adjudicated, we have come to the decision, and this is a verbal decision which will be followed with a very brief written decision, we have come to the conclusion to reject the motion. Definite it's not the case for the Trial Chamber at this point if there is no position on the part of the Prosecution to take those facts as adjudicated. So you are being put on notice that the facts -- relative facts will need to be proved by whoever needs to prove them. And the onus of proof, you know, Mr. Wubben, who carries that onus. The other two, we have the response of the Defence on the protective measures. We got them only minutes before we walked in the courtroom. They are being photocopied and we will discuss them and let you know. But we will let you know before I depart on my way to whatever I have to do abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We did inside file two responses for protective measures and videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have been through them myself but it's really skimming.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed it's just a few minutes ago we handed it to the registry. There is another matter we want to raise before the witness comes in which is this: Yesterday we were served by the Prosecution an exhibit, a photographic exhibit which the Prosecution intends to tender today during the testimony of this witness. We raise the matter now because it's -- it's a matter which in our submission requires serious deliberation on the part of the Chamber and we want to raise it therefore now rather than during the course of examination-in-chief. I'd like to pass up a copy of this photograph so Your Honours can see it. And this photograph which I think it's fair to say is a rather grisly picture of a corpse with what purports to be his sexual organ next to him, and in fact it's even labelled in Serbian to that effect is so -- is so, first of all, prejudicial, but secondly, so lacking in probative value that we thought we should raise the issue before the witness comes in. The question we would pose is this: How is that photograph possibly going to help Your Honours to decide the issues in this trial, in particular the issue of whether there was property damage and whether this accused is in any way responsible for that property damage? How is a photograph of that nature going to help you decide that issue? In our submission it's another try for the Prosecution to bring in grisly, sensationalist, gory material into this trial in a completely appropriate manner because this person is not charged with crimes against the person in these raids and we wonder what the Prosecution has forgotten what they've charged Naser Oric with and if they're trying to drag the trial down into a grisly chamber of horrors. In our submission it's completely inappropriate for the Prosecution to seek to tender this material, and we would say at the very least that if this is going to be tendered that it be done so in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it you, Mr. Di Fazio, or I don't know who is -- we will be leading this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's Mr. Di Fazio, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. What do you seek to prove by this photo? MR. DI FAZIO: The photo, if Your Honours please, shows the results of the attack on the -- the village in the area of Ratkovici. This witness is going to give evidence, I hope, that he was in a small hamlet close to Ratkovici and which was subjected to attack on the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is not watching -- usher, does -- there is no way the witness can hear what we are saying? MR. DI FAZIO: I think he's in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Di Fazio. I just want to make sure he's not in a room where you can follow the conversation or the debate. MR. DI FAZIO: He was just above his small hamlet when the attack started. He ran down, as I understand his evidence, ran down to a small area of uncultivated land just above his village where he hid and watched the attack throughout its duration. During the course of the attack, he saw three of the attacking soldiers, people he knew as people of Muslim ethnicity but more importantly, members of the attacking forces dragged the man from -- depicted in the photograph, from his house, stabbed him to death and then he found the body immediately following the attack with the severed penis inside the man's mouth. A number of other people were killed on that day as well, although not necessarily in the area. Now, the purpose of the photograph is A, to show that the man was not a combatant. It tends to assist that. It also is part and parcel of the story of the attack, and it also bolsters the credibility of this particular witness. He gives an account to you, and he can produce a photo that tends to support what he says to you happened. So for those three reasons, the evidence becomes probative. The other issue raised by my learned friend Mr. Jones is the issue that you have heard repeated so often. Firstly, there's an accusation that it's a descent into grisly sensationalist production of evidence. The Prosecution is only aware that if it were to embark on a foolish and obvious course it would become apparent to you immediately. It wouldn't serve our purposes at all. It just doesn't serve our purposes at all. So from that point of view the Prosecution says it's clearly not going down that particular road. It serves no one's purposes. And also, you're able to put aside the grisly aspect of the photo in your capacity as professional Judges. So for all of those reasons, the photo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From that point of view, Mr. Di Fazio, when we are still students in the third year and we start doing -- that's in my country -- forensic medicine and forensic sciences, we're taken to post-mortems to assist in post-mortems. So this is certainly not going to impress any of us anyway. We are going to suspend the sitting for a short while, a couple of minutes, to discuss this outside, not in the courtroom, and we'll come back with a decision before we start the testimony of this witness. Thank you. --- Short break taken at 9.32 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank -- I thank Mr. Jones, I thank Mr. Di Fazio for explaining the problems attached to the production of this -- the intended production of this photo. We have discussed it amongst ourselves, and we have come to the conclusion that it is relevant to the evidence that the witness will be giving or to the events that he will be testifying upon. However, we feel that in the course of his testimony, if and when the Prosecution comes to the stage of using this document, then you should draw our immediate attention so that we go into private session and it is not -- in other words, we deal with that section in private session. MR. DI FAZIO: That was fully my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I am obliged, Your Honour. There is one other matter in that the photograph is labelled on the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is already in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the witness doesn't see that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's okay, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know how I feel about these things. So can we bring the witness in now? Thank you. How long do you think you require, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps slightly longer than the other more recent witnesses, if Your Honours please. I -- I'm hoping about two hours. He's got two attacks to describe, and -- and -- and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on certain matters you have our go-ahead to lead provided not on matters which are inherently controversial. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand. That won't be a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he performed his compulsory service in the JNA. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not even going to touch that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, just go straight -- MR. DI FAZIO: I will. He's got two attacks and presence after an attack at another of the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: I can raise one matter that made me think about this issue last night and that's this: I wanted to lead him very briefly through some evidence, very briefly, of episodes leading up to the attack in which caused security concerns and tension in the local population. I don't intend to dwell on that very much at all. In fact, I'd like to get through it as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: There's a reason for that, and that will be in relation to questions relating to the defence of these villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: That's the only area that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. We cannot commit ourselves to that for the time being. We'll see how you go about it, and then we will decide whether to let you go on or whether to stop you. Yes. Could you bring Stanisa Stevanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further, I want to make sure that what I am saying in English is being interpreted to you, translated to you, in your own language. Are you receiving interpretation of what I am saying in your own language or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you know why you are here. You've been summoned by the Prosecution to give evidence in this case instituted by them against Naser Oric, and in terms of our Rules, before you even start giving evidence, you are required to enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony here at this trial, you will be testifying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. This is basically what in your country would be -- and in many other countries would be a solemn declaration, also an oath. The text is contained in a piece of paper which Madam Usher is going to hand to you now. May I ask you to read the text allowed, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, witness Stevanovic Stanisa, solemnly declare that I will stay the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Could you please take your seat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you ever given evidence before in your life in a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So more or less, you should know what the procedure is. You're going first to be asked a series of questions by Mr. Di Fazio for the Prosecution. He will then be followed by Madam Vidovic for Naser Oric, and then we see whether we have any further questions for you. We hope to finish with your testimony today, which would then enable you to go back home for the weekend. May I remind you only of one obligation that you have as a result of the solemn declaration that you have made a few minutes ago, namely that the undertaking to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth applies not only when you are being asked questions by the Prosecution who have brought you here but also when you are being asked questions by the Defence. You have no right to say to the Prosecution, "I will answer one way," to the Defence, "I will answer another way because I don't like it." You cannot distinguish or discriminate between the Prosecution and the Defence. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... MR. DI FAZIO: Just before I start, can I alert the technical booth that although I will go into private session for the reasons earlier discussed, there's going to be one reason -- one very short -- I'm going to apply to go into private session very shortly for a very brief period of time just on his personal antecedents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I don't take it we are going into private session now. MR. DI FAZIO: No. Very shortly. I'm going to get to it very shortly. Examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in 1956 in Ratkovici, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to answer. If -- have you heard -- have you heard the question of Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is the answer -- just tell us -- just tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to answer the question. MR. DI FAZIO: You were born in 1956 in Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're going to be there for some time, Mr. Stevanovic. Pull your chair forward, settle down and answer my questions. For most of that time you've lived in Bradjevina which is a small hamlet near Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're a farmer. You raise sheep, cattle. You've got pigs; is that correct? Or had -- this these farm animals?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was back -- this was back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in addition to raising farm animals, you also had a small wood mill or wood-cutting service, and you also had a farm implement that you hired out to other local farmers.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're married and you have a number of children. Can you tell us how many children?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Can we just very briefly go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You know of an eighth one, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure why we're going into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why. We will soon tell us. Usually, this shouldn't be controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think my learned friend should make an application to go into private session or explain what the -- or the reason for that is rather than move into private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already given us an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if it's a matter of the antecedents of this witness I don't see why that should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know we will see. If it's not the case of being in private session we'll revert to open session and we'll go through it again. MR. DI FAZIO: I can deal with it very quickly. I think Your Honours must have a copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we have a copy of his statement but it arrived when we were already gone. MR. DI FAZIO: Page 3, Your Honours. Page 3. Defence have a copy, I hope. Page 3 of the English. Third paragraph. "I should now mention that in 1985." That's the matter I wanted to raise with the witness. I'm going to be very, very brief with it, a matter of two or three questions, and then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see no reason on earth why a witnesses antecedents should be a matter dealt with in private session. These are public trials, and antecedents goes to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the area in which you live is fairly hilly country with farmland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you a hand-written drawing, please. If that can be brought up on -- on the Sanction device. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours have the picture in front of you? Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First things first. Did I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One -- one moment. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take the picture away from the witness, please. Who drew this picture? MR. DI FAZIO: I was about to elicit that evidence if Your Honours please. I did, and the witness marked in the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you showed it to him in the first place, it was not marked? MR. DI FAZIO: I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You -- MR. DI FAZIO: I created this during the course of proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I say is when you were proofing the witness, you didn't actually show him this, what this -- this piece of paper? You showed him something similar to this piece of paper with, I understand, the numbers missing or what? MR. DI FAZIO: No. I -- I spoke to him, got his -- what was his explanation of the local topography or geography, and then following his instructions I drew this map and then I asked him to write in the numbers representing the various hamlets. It's not claimed to be done to scale. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. What I mean to say, in other words, the -- the numbers -- were the numbers inserted by him or by you. MR. DI FAZIO: This witness wrote in the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let's proceed. Give it back to him. Yes, please. Thank you. And he will confirm all this to us. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stevanovic, you've just heard the exchange between myself and the Court, the Trial Chamber. Did I, in fact, create -- write this map with the exception of the numbers that you can actually see on the little map itself?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did we do that together?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's -- you agree that it's not drawn to scale or representing a correct cartographical exercise?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay now, I just want you to comment on the broad features near the area where you live. Near your area there's a main road and you can see it on the little map. Is that the main road that goes up to Bratunac and then south to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leading -- and does that road for much of its course hug the Drina River, stick close to the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Leading off from the main road you can see there two small dirt roads. Are -- in your area do those dirt roads exist?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in between the two small dirt roads that you can see depicted there, is there a small cluster of hills?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are some of the villages close to your hamlet located on the side of those hills and down around the small dirt road?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see there a -- a small dirt road on the left-hand side of the -- of the map leading down to number 1, which is represented by Ratkovici. Is there such a dirt road?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also see numbers 11, 10, and 9. Are they -- do they represent the approximate, very approximate, I should say, very approximate locations of villages of Poznanovici, Dedici, and Potkorjen?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, were they inhabited by people of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The remaining numbers, 2, 8, 7, 6, 5, 3, and 4, and 1, do they correspond to the Serbian villages of Ratkovici, Gornji Ratkovici, Dvorista, Ducici, Magudovici, Bradjevina, Kaludra, and Polimci?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you see the small dirt road that is furthest north towards the top of the drawing, the small dirt road leading off the main road. Along that small dirt road is there a small stream or creek that follows it and heads out towards the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see a very faint dotted line along which the small dirt road leading to Ratkovici goes. Is that -- is there a spine or a crest of hills, the top of the hills, that runs along between the -- the small dirt -- the two small dirt roads with the Muslim villages down on the southern slope and the Serbian villages on the northern slope?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender into evidence that small map. Well, I won't grace it with the word map. Representation of the local area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that that provides -- obviously it's not just that that drawing isn't to scale, it's actively misleading. I don't mean that in a deliberately misleading sense but when one considers the distances there are several kilometres between various of these villages and hamlets and when one sees the Drina and the main road and the size of those representations, one might get the impression that some of these villages are right next door to each other. Provided it's understood that this -- this drawing bears no resemblance to reality, then, fine, it may go in. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I agree with that. I'm not -- I hope I've made abundantly clear it's not to scale and it's basically to represent there are two roads, there's clusters of villages up on one side of the hill, down on the other. And to give you an idea before you start to look at the map that I'm about to produce. That's why I wanted to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the Chamber thank you both, Mr. Jones and Mr. Di Fazio for clarifying what we had almost taken for -- not almost, but we certainly had taken for granted. But anyway, this will be P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is being admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P401. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to show you a map, and I'd like it placed on the ELMO because I'm going to ask you to mark it, which I hope is a little more elegant than my drawing. MR. DI FAZIO: Could the witness be shown this particular document. You can also get it up on Sanction -- I'm sorry, just the ELMO. Excuse me, Ms. Usher, can I have a look, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm also going to supply to you, Mr. Stevanovic, two marking pens, one in pink and one in blue. All right. Okay. Now, I just want you to highlight with the pink pen. If you can draw on this map with the pink pen. I want you to highlight some of the little towns and villages that you might mention so the Trial Chamber can see where they are. First of all, can you see a place called Vranesevici, and can you highlight that in pink? Just put -- write in pink, right through the name of the little village, right across the name. You wouldn't obscure the lettering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Highlight it, in other words. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Highlight it. Drag the pink across the name Vranesevici.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's it. Now that's what I want you to do with the rest of it. Now, show the Trial Chamber where a place called Magudovici is?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now show us where a small village called Kaludra is.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now a place called Polimci.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just although it's already indicated, mark Ducici and Dvorista.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now look over on the right-hand side of the -- of the -- of the map. Right-hand side. Right over on the right-hand side and down to the bottom third of the -- of the map and we start to see -- MR. DI FAZIO: A bit further, Ms. Usher, if we can. More to the right. No, the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other way. The right. MR. DI FAZIO: The other way. More. That's it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the right-hand side down towards the bottom you see three letters, FAK. Do you see those letters there, Mr. Stevanovic? Do you see them? Well, let me ask you this, where would Fakovici be approximately?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Right here underneath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We'll deal with that later. Now, on -- is there a creek or a small stream that runs, as you've mentioned already, from the area around Ducici down towards the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now using the blue can you mark that stream that runs along from Ducici and past Dvorista down to the main road and to the Drina. You can just see it in blue. I'm hoping the blue marker will make it a bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally pick up the pink pen again and mark on that map the approximate location of your hamlet Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That I would like you to put in the form of a cross and put your initials next to it, please. Put B, B, with -- to indicate. And then put a dash and your initials, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and there will be Exhibit P402. So this is being admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P402. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I may show you one more map. This time I won't ask you to mark anything. Again, if it could be very briefly put on the ELMO. Now, I think on this map you can see Fakovici, can't you? Can you perhaps mark it? I will ask you to mark it. Just mark the area where Fakovici is, again, in pink texter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, this -- this is always why the -- why I am against having them pre-marked, because you will see he marks Fakovici where it is written, not where it is. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I appreciate that. Perhaps we'll leave Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just show us where Polimci is marked. And Kaludra. And I think over on the left-hand side you can see Ducici?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be P403. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early -- early 1992, about how many households were in the hamlet of Bradjevina? About how many people?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Twelve households and about 45 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of them farmers with their own cows and sheep and pigs and so on?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to very briefly, and I emphasise the word "briefly," describe to Their Honours various episodes that took place in early 1992 in your area. In early 1992, were you made aware of some episode involving a bus, a bus not being allowed into a terminal because of the people it was carrying?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again very briefly, in the space of a few sentences, just tell Their Honours what that was about, as far as you're aware.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was in Bratunac, and rockets, missiles, were being transported on the bus. When I got there, when I wanted to get on the bus, barricades had been put up and they wouldn't allow the bus into the terminal, so they sent it right back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Who -- were there any members of any ethnicity on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The name of the bus was actually Raketa or rocket. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zicko, a man named Zicko from Zapolje and another one from Zanjevo. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there weapons on this bus or not, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's a bus commuting between Belgrade and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it was -- barricades were put up and the bus wasn't allowed into the terminal. Were there members of any one particular ethnic group on the bus?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: How am I supposed to know? There were all sorts of people on that bus, whoever the passengers happened to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, did that incident become well known in your local area?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was on the bus on that day too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did the fact of the bus being not permitted into the terminal become well known in your local area? Was it --

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When is the Orthodox Easter? When was the Orthodox Easter in 1992? Can you recall? Just approximate. The month will do.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in early April, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. Did you in early April go to a Muslim village called Mocevici?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you going there in order to purchase walnut trees?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There did you see barricades erected?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these barricades over roads leading into and out of the ridge?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you worried about what you saw at Mocevici, the erection of barricades? Did that cause you any concerns?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to turn your mind to May the 6th, 1992. On that occasion were -- were you aware of any persons being killed or assassinated?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, what happened?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that they had been killed at Jadar, but I didn't see that. I was in Ratkovici. But we heard that some people had been killed at Jadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your children were living with you at that time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of this particular killing in -- in May, did you do anything in respect of your children?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I took my children to Vranesevici village to stay with my relative, Milisav Ignjatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that because you thought they'd be safer there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view and from -- not in your view, but can you tell the Chamber if your perception was in early 1992 that matters were worsening in Bosnia and that ethnic relations were deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1992, was a man named Milisav Milanovic also assassinated?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, did that contribute to the worsening climate that you've spoken of?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early June of 1992, was there an attack by Muslim forces on a village called Oparci?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oparci, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oparci, sorry?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again did that influence this worsening climate that you've described?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for telling us of that. I wanted to ask you about any system of guarding Bradjevina. Was there ever a system of guarding Bradjevina mounted by the men of -- of the small hamlet of Bradjevina? Did it ever come into being?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About when was that done, approximately?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as incidents began occurring in February or March. A little at first, and then increasingly more and more guards as incidents kept happening throughout the villages. You heard that someone had been killed in one village and someone was set alight in a different village. We only came on the 27th, and many villages had been set alight by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what was formed and how did it operate? And I'm now talking about Bradjevina, your little town, your hamlet. I'm only talking about Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Each of the villages had its own village guard and for individual houses too. We didn't have any special units to do that. Everyone guarded their own house and their own property. The women had gone, and only the men were left. We were only 12 in our village, so that's all we could afford in terms of providing village guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the women leave Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st, when Ratkovici fell, and all the other villages and hamlets in Ratkovici local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up until that time had the women been living in the hamlets and villages around Ratkovici, including Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 21st, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Bradjevina, how many men would stand guard?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were only 12 there. All the rest had crossed into Serbia. The young people and the elderly. Only 12 of us remained who were sort of the right age. We looked after the livestock, the farm animals, and we stood guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, was there a similar system of guards as you had in Bradjevina in places, the surrounding hamlets like Ratkovici, Gornji Ratkovici, Dvorista, Ducici, Polimci, Kaludra, Vranesevici, those places? Was there a similar system of local occupants of the villages and hamlets setting up guard systems as you had in Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly they had guards too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again return your attention to Bradjevina and your guard system in your hamlet. Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We did have some weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of weaponry did you have?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were all sorts of weapons, machine-guns, rifles, PAP rifles, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I just want you to convey the correct picture to the Trial Chamber. You said there are about 12 men. Did each of them have more than one weapon or only one weapon?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I gave you two choices. Did each of them have more than one weapon or did each month have only one weapon?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know what it was like. We had to buy weapons in 1992, and whoever could afford one had one, had a good one, and whoever couldn't afford a good weapon had a poor weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in Bradjevina? What did the men have there, what sort of weaponry? Bradjevina I'm talking about, not the other places. Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Individually, I can't enumerate. I know what I had at the time. I can't tell you what the others had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you have?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a 48-millimetre rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is that an automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did other men from Bradjevina own Schmeisser sub-machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think Milenko Stevanovic had a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you --

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were semi-automatic rifles, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Where did you personally get your weapon?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A man brought it over for me from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a local branch of the SDS party operating in the area?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Slavko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever play, as far as you're aware, any role in the distribution of weapons in your area?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what he did, as far as you're aware, to bring about this distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, since we were at a distance from Fakovici, about ten kilometres, between five and ten, we stood guard in the village and we just looked after our livestock there. We hardly ever went to Fakovici, but I heard from people that weapons were being bought and sold in his cafe. That was the extent of my knowledge. I also heard that he was president of the SDS for the Fakovici area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's be clear about what you heard. You heard that you could go to Slavko Jovanovic's cafe and there you could buy a weapon. Is that what you heard? What I want to know is whether you heard you could go there and buy a weapon --

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that you could go there and just get a weapon, just get one given to you for nothing?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the beginning. You had to buy one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you get your weapon, the actual gun that you held in your hands in Bradjevina, from anyone associated with the SDS or through that assistance of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Nikola Stanojevic came to see me and he had come over from Fakovici, and he asked me -- I asked him whether I could have one and he promised it and he brought it to me eventually. I paid one million dinars for that rifle at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Stanojevic come over to your place on this occasion to discuss the issue of weaponry or did he come to your place on this occasion for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: He came, and he was looking for -- for a flashlight because it was night and he had been late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And did you -- talk turn to the issue of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to you about the availability of weapons? What did he tell you you could do to get a gun?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: He said that since I was not friends with Slavko, I had returned from prison in 1990, I was not a member of the SDS, and I was not in friendly relations with anyone from Fakovici. I was in the hills, so I asked him whether he could get one for me because they were friends at the time, and he brought one over for me then. I gave him a million dinars in return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, were you ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us about the organisation of village guards in the -- your village and the surrounding hamlets. Can I ask you this: Did you dig any trenches in and around Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did, small trenches. Well, we had to take shelter somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's okay. I just want to know what you did. How many trenches did you dig around Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Local villagers dug them?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't precisely go there, but they must have been the ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ever see similar trenches in the other hamlets and villages in your area, the ones I've just mentioned to you, Ducici, Dvorista, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to those villages at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bradjevina did the men organise themselves into shifts so that at night some would go out and some would rest? Did you have shifts organised?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Okay. And while we're on protective measures, I want to ask you this: In the period of time leading up to the 21st of June, did people who lived in Ducici and Dvorista, Ducici and Dvorista, go anywhere at night?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not through Bradjevina. I heard that they were going to Ratkovici and the guys from Ducici they couldn't back in their own village because there were very few of them. Ducici had two or three men in each of the gardens but there were several men over there as far as I heard. They would go to Ratkovici in the evening and go back in the morning to attend to their livestock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the occupants of those two hamlets, most of them, at night would go down to Ratkovici for safety and then go back and work their fields during the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to think of the period from early 1992, very early 1992, up until the 21st of June, 1992, that period of time, the first six months or so. In that time, did your Bradjevina village guard ever have any contact with the VRS or the JNA? And by that I mean did you receive any training, equipment, advisors? Were any systems set up for you to contact the VRS in order to assist them in any way? Any form of contact of any nature whatsoever between the VRS, the JNA, and your village guard?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for contacts between the army and ourselves, there were none. As far as I know, in Ruljevici, in the school building there had been a meeting back at the beginning. I'm not sure about the specific time, February or March. Which month I don't know much that's when they went to Ruljevici, to the school, not all of them, some of them had remained in the village and there was a meeting of some sort over there but I don't know what sort of meeting exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who went to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everyone from all the hamlets. Some people went and some people remained back in the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is this village of Ruljevici from --

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From Bradjevina, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, up to two or three kilometres, not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you this: Following this meeting that you became aware of, were you -- did you see or observe anywhere in your area, anywhere at all, any form of contact between villagers in the village guard and the VRS or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I may just finish on this note: Your village guard and all the other village guards in the area, I want to know what equipment did they have. Were they equipped with binoculars, radios, helmets, uniforms, any of the usual paraphernalia of soldiers apart from their personal weaponry?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have anything like that, only what we wore, our own civilian clothes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's almost 10.30. That's a natural break in my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. We will have a 25-minute break. How much longer do you think you'll require? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy to say I'm going faster than I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you because I have gone through the main statement and I think you have gone quite far already. So I'm trying to -- to help myself and the other two Judges and the Defence -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I would say, just weighing up my notes, it's going to take me probably about another hour, hour and a quarter or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what about you, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I'll need about two hours at least. That much is certain, Your Honour, and you will see for yourselves why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically if we start, say, at 11.00, we have an hour and a half, then another three-quarters of another. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think -- I -- I respectfully don't think we're going to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an important witness. I mean, I -- anyway, we'll discuss this after the break, but -- we'll talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed. Please try to make an effort to cut down as much as you can so that we see if we can hopefully finish with this witness today. If not, I am afraid, wishing that the weather in The Hague will remain nice, you will have a nice weekend over here if we don't finish with you today. Mr. Di Fazio, let's not lose more time. Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to turn your attention to the 21st of June, 1992. On that occasion were you in Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At about 5.00 a.m. in the morning, or early in the morning, were you carrying out the guard duties you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a trench?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time of the morning in that area, was there a fog?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see at all the surrounding hamlets or not? Did you have the -- or was the fog too thick?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes, but later it cleared up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did anything happen that morning?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's not beat about the bush. Was the -- was there an attack carried out on the villages and surrounding hamlets?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not on my village, but the five hamlets, Donji Ratkovici, Ducici, Polimci, and Gornji Ratkovici, yes. These were five hamlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your position in the trench, what could you see as the attack started?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, we couldn't see because there was fog. Later when it lifted, we could see Gornji Ratkovici, Polimci, and Dvorista. We could not see Donji Ratkovici and Ducici because they were behind the hill in relation to my village and you could not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fog or no fog, from your position you would never have been able to see Ducici and Gornji Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when the fog lifted you could see the other three that you mentioned. How far away --

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away from your position in the trench is the furthest of those three hamlets, Polimci, Gornji Ratkovici, and Dvorista? Which one is furthest and how far away from your position in the trench?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Gornji Ratkovici is the farthest away, and Polimci and Dvorista are closer. As the crow flies, it's shorter. If you were to measure it by going down, going into the river and then going up it's longer, but as the crow flies it's not more than three kilometres. But if you actually take the road, then it's about five kilometres from one village to the next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you make out and see figures of people at that distance in those places, Polimci, Gornji Ratkovici, and Dvorista?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see fires burning anywhere?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see fires?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We saw them in Gornji Ratkovici, Polimci, and Dvorista, but from Gornji -- from Donji Ratkovici and Dvorista you could only see smoke. And all the barns and the outbuildings that were in the fields, they were all burning, all the way down to the river. This was on the other side of my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say -- I'll withdraw that. Did you see any soldiers that day?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From Polimci down by the fields when they were burning the stables in the fields. And then when we were withdrawing from Gornji Ratkovici and Dvorista towards Mocevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what could you see those soldiers doing in the fields?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them doing anything in the fields, but I did see them taking the cattle away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were they in the fields and not in the three hamlets of Polimci, Gornji Ratkovici, and Dvorista when the cattle were being taken away? In other words, were they outside those hamlets in the field taking away the cattle? Is that a correct picture?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was morning, so the cattle was in the stables, and they were being released. So that was the time that -- at 5.00 in the morning when the cattle was being let out from the stables, but that wasn't the usual time for them to already be in the fields. When the attack occurred, that was the time when they were just being let out into the fields to graze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, think about this: You've told the Chamber it was foggy in the morning, okay, and you've told the Chamber you couldn't see figures over in the villages and hamlets three kilometres away. How could you see that cattle were being released from -- from barns and their pens? Could -- that's my question.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the fog lifted later, because at first we couldn't see. At one point the fog lifted. After the firing and everything it had lifted. That's when we were able to see. But in the beginning, we couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just give us a bit more detail about what you could see. Were people who were letting cattle out of the barns and pens and so on, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were both soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they herd and take away the cattle?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall in which direction?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From Dvorista they were going towards Mocevici and from Gornji Ratkovici they were going up along the slope above Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the buildings were emptied of cattle, did anything happen to the buildings?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever actually see how fire was set to the buildings?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the villages, you mean? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what about in the fields? Were there any structures in the fields?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me get this straight. From your position, you could see over into the hamlets, and you could see fires occurring in the hamlets, but you couldn't see how they started. Correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in the fields you had a closer view. Could you there see how fire started in the various structures in the fields?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because when you enter the barn or the stable, you cannot see it. You can only see the smoke once it's alight. So you cannot see if somebody goes inside to set it on fire. You can just see once it begins to burn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see soldiers and civilians going inside these structures that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers and civilians exit these structures that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the exit, did you see the structures that you have just mentioned ablaze?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of -- throughout the day -- throughout the day, was there any artillery or heavy shelling coming from any direction or any forces, Serb forces or Muslim forces, any bombs or bombing of the area, or was it simply rifle and automatic weapon fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You could hear some shooting in those villages, but I don't know where the shooting came from, but you could hear some shooting, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We've heard that, shooting. And by shooting do you mean from small weapons, hand-held weaponry?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It sounded like bombs or some sort of dull sound. I don't know if it was bombs or shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not really that knowledgeable about weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't suppose it should be that difficult to distinguish between just rifle shootings -- shooting and -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll ask -- perhaps I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And shells and proper artillery. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any explosions, any explosions? I'm not talking from gunfire from small rifles, machine-guns held by men, by soldiers. Did you see any explosions? And I'm not talking about fire either. Explosions, explosions that might be caused by bombs or heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You could hear something in Ratkovici, something of that. I don't know if that was mortars or bombs or some other kind of weapon. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Ducici, Dvorista, Polimci, Kaludra, anywhere of those areas could you see any explosions caused by bombs?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On that particular day, were the hamlets of Bradjevina, Kaludra, and Magudovici attacked or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In addition to seeing cattle led away, did you see anyone, any soldiers or civilians, and I'm now talking about the 21st, okay being the 21st of June, did you see any civilians or soldiers carrying away stuff, food, appliances, anything like that at all?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. Following -- just one last question while we're on the 21st. Did you remain in your trench observing these events throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the duration of the attack?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The attack was short, that attack on Ratkovici and those other four hamlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 27th of June, was the area attacked once again?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because there was nobody there any more in those villages. They had burned down, and they were abandoned. Only Magudovici, Bradjevina, and Kaludra were attacked. That was on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Right. Right. Now, in between the 21st and the 27th, did you go down to Ducici and Dvorista and the other hamlets and see what damage had occurred or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell the Trial Chamber on what basis you make the assertion that those villages had been burned down and abandoned? I'm talking about the villages attacked on the 21st of June. How do you know that? Why would you say that to the Trial Judges?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because you could see from my village that they had been burned down, that there were no roofs on the buildings any more. All of them had been burned down. You could see from my village the three hamlets where everything had burned down. You could see everything had burned down. There were no roofs left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the extent of the damage that you could see in each of those three hamlets from your position in Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was 100 per cent damage. Everything that people had was damaged. All the buildings were burned. The damage was 100 per cent. The cattle was driven away. Everything that the farmers had was destroyed 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Following this attack on the 21st of June, did your wife go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: She went to Vranesevici to see the children off to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do anything with your cattle?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: First I took the cattle down to Grabovicka Rijeka, the part of the cattle that I did not manage to save. And then on the 26th, on Friday I returned to the village again, and then on the 27th there was the attack so whatever was there of the cattle was driven away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it from your last answer that on the 21st some of our own cattle were taken away during the course of the attack?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. None of my cattle was taken away on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said that the part of the cattle that you managed to save, you took them down to Grabovicka Rijeka. Were any of your cattle stolen at all on the 21st? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was stolen by the Serbs in Podrinje. Those of us from Brdo who took the cattle down to Podrinje, that cattle was stolen. They had started to take that cattle and slaughter it and they had taken it to their land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who, because I feel a little bit after confusion in the air here. Was the cattle stolen by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it was. When we took the cattle to Grabovicka Rijeka, to Vranesevici, they started to steal this cattle away. Then on the 26th we returned again to our property because we were thinking that we would not be attacked. So then on the 27th when the attack occurred, all that had been saved from the people down there was then driven away by these others, by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's -- that's clear now. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser has got a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, how was it? Were the cattle already stolen while it was still in Bradjevina or was it stolen after you had let it down to what was called Grabovicka Rijeka, after the 21st of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th of June, we took it to Grabovicka Rijeka, the cattle. And then from the 21st to the 26th, the local people there, Serbs, stole the cattle. They stole from everybody, more from some, less from others. Those people who were -- some people had all of their cattle slaughtered. For example, Ljubisa Popovic, all of his sleep were slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, your cattle was not stolen while still in Bradjevina but it was stolen in the time when it was down to Grabovicka. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Not all of the cattle was stolen. A part was stolen in Grabovicka Rijeka, and then the rest when it came back, when I brought it back was then stolen, because I had over a hundred head of cattle, and then I returned -- when it came back there was about 36 or something, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did I understand you rightly that the first part of your cattle which were stolen were stolen by Serbs who had lost their own sheeps and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not lose their cattle because they were not attacked then. They had their own cattle, but they were also stealing our cattle, the ones we had driven down from Brdo.
